references.text: "You shall not show partiality to people" – God's impartiality is the basis for the accusation that Jesus "does not take account of persons" ([ref:Deut 10:17|Deuteronomy 10:17]). The Hebrew expression for "lifting up the face" (נָשָׂא פָנִים) lies behind the Greek λαμβάνεις πρόσωπον.
The warning in [ref:2 Chron 19:7|2 Chronicles 19:7] that there is no injustice or partiality with the Lord forms the background for the expression of not "taking account of persons".
Job describes God as one who "does not show partiality to princes over the poor" ([ref:Job 34:19|Job 34:19]), a motif that the spies play on when they flatter Jesus.

The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 22:16|Matthew 22:16] recounts the same event where the disciples of the Pharisees and the Herodians ask Jesus the same question with similar flattery, saying that he teaches the way of God in truth.
The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 12:14|Mark 12:14] uses almost identical wording: "you do not look at people's outward appearance, but teach the way of God in truth".

Nicodemus addresses Jesus as "Teacher" (διδάσκαλε) and acknowledges that he has come from God ([ref:John 3:2|John 3:2]), similarly to how the spies here address Jesus as "Teacher" and acknowledge his trustworthiness.

Jesus says that whoever seeks honor for the one who sent him is truthful, and there is no unrighteousness in him ([ref:John 7:18|John 7:18]). This confirms what the spies say – that he teaches the way of God in truth.
Paul writes that "God does not show partiality" ([ref:Gal 2:6|Galatians 2:6]), using directly the expression πρόσωπον λαμβάνει, the same one used about Jesus in this verse.

The context in [ref:Luke 20:20|Luke 20:20] explains that those who asked the question were spies pretending to be sincere, in order to catch Jesus in his words – the flattery in verse 21 is thus an attempt to trap him.
